strengths: The paper addresses an important question: why categorical distributional RL can outperform expected-value methods. It engages relevant prior work on distributional learning, optimization, statistical benefits, and exploration.
The conditional return-density decomposition and categorical–histogram KL-loss equivalence provide a useful algebraic perspective on separating a mean-bin likelihood term from distribution fitting.

The experiments cover eight Atari games and eight continuous-control environments, with multiple seeds, atom-count ablations, and combinations with policy entropy regularization. Reporting both improvements and interference provides useful empirical information, and the appendices include pseudocode and several implementation details.
weaknesses: The central connection between critic-loss decomposition and intrinsic exploration is not established. Equations 6–8 explicitly introduce a cross-entropy reward bonus, but decomposing the ordinary distributional critic loss does not show that its policy optimizes this augmented objective. Standard risk-neutral distributional action selection uses expected returns. Theorem 1 concerns the newly defined bonus-based policy iteration with fixed q, rather than establishing the claimed mechanism in C51 or distributional actor-critic learning. This gap substantially weakens the main contribution.

The principal ablation does not remove distributional information as claimed. Appendix K.2 replaces the target p with the residual μ; decreasing ε removes mass from the mean bin and increases mass elsewhere. For example, p=(0.25,0.5,0.25) on three equally spaced bins becomes μ=(0.475,0.05,0.475) at ε=0.1. This amplifies the tails rather than approaching a mean-only target. Consequently, the performance degradation in Figure 3 can reflect target distortion and does not isolate the benefit of the proposed regularization.

Cross-entropy is not a pure measure of distribution mismatch: H(μ,q)=H(μ)+KL(μ||q). Even at q=μ, the proposed bonus retains the target entropy. Across states, it can therefore favor accurately modeled, inherently stochastic outcomes rather than underestimated uncertainty. The paper needs to distinguish irreducible randomness from estimation error and demonstrate when this bonus supports useful exploration.

Several theoretical steps require correction. Proposition 3 assumes that representing the full target also permits representing its single-bin component, which does not follow for an arbitrary function class. Equation 35 establishes Θ(Δ), not the claimed o(Δ), convergence. Appendix F invokes Banach's fixed-point theorem after proving only non-expansiveness under KL. The DERAC derivation in Equation 40 also expands the squared expression incorrectly and discards an interaction term without a justification applicable to the learning iterates. These issues reduce confidence in the technical support.

The experiments measure returns but do not directly test the proposed exploration mechanism through visitation coverage, uncertainty estimation, or controlled environmental stochasticity. Changing the critic loss also changes optimization, representation learning, and value-estimation errors. Controls using shared replay data or classification-based scalar-value learning would help distinguish these explanations. Likewise, performance interactions with SAC entropy do not by themselves demonstrate competing exploration directions.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the supplied hyperparameter table. The manuscript provides no identifiable code link and leaves important details insufficiently specified, including categorical support bounds and Atari preprocessing, exploration, and evaluation settings. These details matter particularly for reproducing the target-redistribution ablation and interpreting its sensitivity.
